title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai, an AI transcription service used by millions, is accused of automatically recording virtual meetings without notifying all participants and using those recordings to train its AI systems. The class-action lawsuit alleges the practice violated users' privacy even when some participants had not consented, violating state and federal wiretap laws. This is a deployment failure where a system collected data from interactions involving non-users who had no opportunity to opt out.

The company's stated defense rests on a consent box in its privacy policy, but the lawsuit challenges whether this consent was informed or effective for all parties to a recorded conversation. The failure occurred at the point where the system was deployed to automatically join and record meetings without human review of whether all participants had agreed. Catching this would have required either restricting recordings to meetings where all participants explicitly consented in real time, or requiring human verification before any recording began.

It is not established whether Otter's data anonymization claims are accurate, whether the company intentionally deceived users, or what the legal outcome will be.

summary:
A federal class-action lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit alleges that Otter's software automatically joins virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams and records discussions to train its artificial intelligence systems, often without notifying all participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was violated when he discovered Otter had secretly recorded a confidential conversation. The lawsuit contends this practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

Otter.ai serves approximately 25 million users and has processed over 1 billion meetings since its 2016 founding. The company claims its privacy policy grants permission for AI training when users check a consent box, though the lawsuit argues many users are still deceived. Several privacy incidents have surfaced recently, including reports of Otter sharing sensitive business details with third parties and concerns about potential access by foreign governments. The company maintains it anonymizes data before using it for AI improvement but provides no public explanation of this process, which the lawsuit questions.
